newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac raps feuding as France's Juppe under fire.
newsitem.headline: Chirac raps feuding as France's Juppe under fire.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac told his ruling coalition on Wednesday to stop squabbling as suggestions mounted that Prime Minister Alain Juppe should go even if he leads the centre-right to an election victory.

Juppe's fate jumped to the centre of the campaign for the May 25-June 1 parliamentary election as Chirac chaired a cabinet meeting before leaving for a state visit to China, prompting him to warn ministers not to let polemics overshadow the issues.

"Unfortunately, the serious debate worthy of our democracy...is often masked by polemics and soundbites, from both the coalition and the opposition, which end up being the only things the public remembers," government spokesman Alain Lamassoure quoted Chirac as telling the cabinet.
The most unpopular premier since 1958 because of budget austerity, record unemployment and an image as a cold technocrat, Juppe is under fire both from foes and some allies.
Ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing repeated on television on Tuesday night that it would be dangerous to ignore the fact that the voters wanted to be "governed differently".

Confirming other surveys, a Sofres opinion poll for the weekly Le Pelerin showed that Gaullist National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin was the voters' favourite for the premiership should the right win, with Juppe trailing far behind.
"If Seguin is not a candidate to succeed Juppe, then hens have teeth", the popular daily France-Soir said.

Seguin, who has toned down criticism of a single European currency during the campaign, spoke out in defence of his long-time rival in an interview released on Wednesday, saying Juppe was the victim of "a manhunt unworthy of our democracy".
Many of Juppe's own allies see him as a liability even though opinion polls forecast a comfortable centre-right win.
The latest Ifop poll saw support for the right rising to 48 percent from 43, with the left dropping to 38 percent from 41.
The polls buoyed French financial markets, with the Paris Bourse CAC40 index rising more than two percent to briefly touch an all-time record of 2,781.87.
Urban Affairs Minister Eric Raoult said at the weekend that Seguin would make a good premier.

After one poll suggested most voters would prefer a prime minister from the private sector to a professional politician, ex-justice minister Pierre Mehaignerie suggested the chairman of national airline Air France, Christian Blanc.
The left-wing opposition is trying to make the most of the current incumbent's unpopularity by warning of "five more years of Juppe" if the coalition is re-elected.
Juppe, 51, may have been referring obliquely to rivalry with Seguin, 54, when he made a rather bitter comment on his own unpopularity in a radio interview on Tuesday.
"Is it better to have a jovial fat man who does not know the issues or a thin man, slightly less jovial, who does?" he asked.
No jovial fat man has yet stepped forward to take offence.

Juppe has said if he had to choose between the premiership and his elected office as mayor of Bordeaux under a proposed move to bar politicians from holding two executive posts, he would prefer to stay in Bordeaux.
The left said speculation about Juppe's replacement was a ploy from the right to make voters believe he would leave.

The Communist daily L'Humanite called Seguin "a decoy" and Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin recalled that the last conservative prime minister to win an election, centrist Raymond Barre, had kept his job.
"They are trying to make us believe otherwise this time. In fact, if the right wins Juppe will stay on," he told reporters.
The Sofres poll said that 26 percent of voters favoured Seguin and 21 percent ex-premier Edouard Balladur as premier compared to only eight percent for Juppe if the right wins.

The Ifop poll saw Juppe still lagging behind Jospin in voters' preferences although he improved his score to 36 percent from 33. Jospin dropped to 38 percent from 40, and 20 percent said they wanted neither Juppe nor Jospin.
